Q: PERMANOVA sample size limitations A:

A rule of thumb is to have 10-15 subjects per parameter to be estimated. You have 5 subjects. So trying to use any sort of ANOVA to establish a statistical measure of difference is going to be difficult and unlikely to allow consideration of anything like 24 features to be evaluated independently. You would be better advised to to use such a small sample as an exploratory dataset. As such trying to identify highly correlated features is a sensible method. It’s unclear what these measurements with widely varying numbers of data points actually represent. Frequencies? Some sort of sequential measure? Intensities in octaves? Chords? It occurs to me that bird call identification might be somehow parallel to this task.

Q: /usr/bin/node: 1: Syntax error: ")" unexpected A:

In WSL 1, the issue appears to be that the emulated kernel is trying to run the Node binary as though it were text instead of as an ELF binary.

None of the previous answers worked for me in WSL 1, so I switched to using the wrapper script below instead.

Create the ~/bin directory, and then put this in ~/bin/node-wsl1-wrapper:

#!/bin/sh

# node-wsl1-wrapper
# Wraps the NodeJS binary to ensure it's loaded with the correct binary loader.

set -eu

NVM_DIR="${NVM_DIR:-$HOME/.nvm}"
TOOL="$(basename "$0")"

resolve_version() {
  for alias_name in current default; do
    alias_file="$NVM_DIR/alias/$alias_name"
    if [ -r "$alias_file" ]; then
      version="$(cat "$alias_file")"
      if [ -n "$version" ] && [ "$version" != "system" ]; then
        printf '%s\n' "$version"
        return 0
      fi
    fi
  done
  echo "$TOOL: no valid nvm alias found" >&2
  exit 1
}

VERSION="$(resolve_version)"
NODE_ROOT="$NVM_DIR/versions/node/$VERSION"
REAL_NODE="$NODE_ROOT/bin/node"

if [ ! -x "$REAL_NODE" ]; then
  echo "$TOOL: missing Node binary: $REAL_NODE" >&2
  exit 1
fi

case "$TOOL" in
  node)
    exec /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 "$REAL_NODE" "$@"
    ;;
  npm)
    exec /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 \
      "$REAL_NODE" \
      "$NODE_ROOT/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js" \
      "$@"
    ;;
  npx)
    exec /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 \
      "$REAL_NODE" \
      "$NODE_ROOT/lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npx-cli.js" \
      "$@"
    ;;
  *)
    echo "Unsupported tool name: $TOOL" >&2
    exit 1
    ;;
esac

You'll need to setup some NodeJS version aliases (current and a default fallback):

nvm alias current "$(nvm version node)"
nvm alias default "$(nvm version node)"

You'll also need to add $HOME/bin to your path, before the path entries that NVM adds. Put this at the end of your shell RC file (e.g., ~/.bashrc or ~/.bash_profile):

export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"

Then, run these commands:

source ~/.bashrc

chmod +x ~/bin/node-wsl1-tool

ln -sf "$HOME/bin/node-wsl1-wrapper" ~/bin/node
ln -sf "$HOME/bin/node-wsl1-wrapper" ~/bin/npm
ln -sf "$HOME/bin/node-wsl1-wrapper" ~/bin/npx

# Clear shell command resolver cache.
hash -r

The following commands should then work correctly:

which node
which npm
which npx
node -v
npm -v
npx -v

For example:

$ which node
/home/guyep/bin/node

$ which npm
/home/guyep/bin/npm

$ which npx
/home/guyep/bin/npx

$ node -v
v24.14.0

$ npm -v
11.9.0

$ npx -v
11.9.0

If you use NVM to upgrade or change which version of NodeJS you are using, be sure to re-run the alias command:

nvm alias current "$(nvm version node)"

Q: How to display two decimal points in Python when a number is perfectly divisible? A:

The division works and returns adequate precision in result.

So your problem is just about visualization or exactly:

  • string-representation of floating-point numbers

Formatting a decimal

You can use string-formatting for that. For example in Python 3, use f-strings:

twoFractionDigits = f"{result:.2f}"

or print(f"{result:.2f}")

The trick does .2f, a string formatting literal or format specifier that represents a floating-point number (f) with two fractional digits after decimal-point (.2).

See also:

  • Fixed digits after decimal with f-strings
  • How to format a floating number to fixed width in Python

Try on the Python-shell:

Python 3.6.9 (default, Dec  8 2021, 21:08:43) 
[GCC 8.4.0] on linux
Type "help", "copyright", "credits" or "license" for more information.
>>> import math
>>> a=1.175                            #value of a after some division
>>> result = math.floor(a*100)/100
>>> result
1.17
>>> print(result)
1.17
>>> a=25/5                                   #Now a is perfectly divisible
>>> result = math.floor(a*100)/100
>>> result
5.0
>>> print(result)
5.0
>>> print(f"{result:.2f}")
5.00

Formatting a decimal as percentage

Similar you can represent the ratio as percentage: print(f"{result:.2f} %")

prints:

5.00 %

A formatting shortcut for percentage can be: print(f"{25/100:.2%}") Which converts the result of 25/100 == 0.25 to:

25.00%

Note: The formatting-literal .2% automatically converts from ratio to percentage with 2 digits after the decimal-point and adds the percent-symbol.

Formatting a decimal with specific scale (rounded or truncated ?)

Now the part without rounding-off, just truncation. As example we can use the repeating decimal, e.g. 1/6 which needs to be either rounded or truncated (cut-off) after a fixed number of fractional digits - the scale (in contrast to precision).

>>> print(f"{1/6:.2}")
0.17
>>> print(f"{1/6:.2%}")
16.67%

Note how the formatted string is not truncated (to 0.16) but rounded (to 0.17). Here the scale was specified inside formatting-literal as 2 (after the dot).

See also:

  • Truncate to three decimals in Python
  • How do I interpret precision and scale of a number in a database?
  • What is the difference between precision and scale?

Formatting many decimals in fixed width (leading spaces)

Another example is to print multiple decimals, like in a column as right-aligned, so you can easily compare them.

Then use string-formatting literal 6.2f to add leading spaces (here a fixed-width of 6):

>>> print(f"{result:6.2f}")
  5.00
>>> print(f"{100/25*100:6.2f}")
400.00
>>> print(f"{25/100*100:6.2f}")
 25.00

See also

All the formatting-literals demonstrated here can also be applied using

  • old-style %-formatting (also known as "Modulo string formatting") which was inherited from printf method of C language. Benefit: This way is also compatible with Python before 3.6).
  • new-style .format method on strings (introduced with Python 3)

See theherk's answer which demonstrates those alternatives.

Learn more about string-formatting in Python:

  • Real Python: Python 3's f-Strings: An Improved String Formatting Syntax (Guide)
  • Real Python: Python String Formatting Best Practices

Q: Limiting floats to two decimal points A:

Use

print "{:.2f}".format(a)

instead of

print "{0:.2f}".format(a)

Because the latter may lead to output errors when trying to output multiple variables (see comments).

Q: How can I enable dark mode for the Windows Forms Designer in JetBrains Rider? A:

No, Rider does not currently support a dark theme for the Windows Forms Designer.

The IDE theme and editor color scheme can be dark, but the WinForms Designer surface itself is not themeable at the moment. You can set the form's BackColor and ForeColor manually, but that changes the form being designed, not the designer environment.

So this is currently not supported rather than a missing setting.
